meta.title: Chiesi Data Bootcamp Learning Journey — Wisdom → Imagination → Socio-technical Learning → Capability → Practice → Analytics → Cases
meta.subtitle: A dense knowledge lattice for understanding the Chiesi professional-learning journey: technological capability expands the perception of possibility; data bootcamp practices convert business ambiguity into evidence artefacts, prototypes and cross-functional action.
meta.domainName: Professional data learning, organisational agility and data-enabled transformation in pharmaceutical business contexts
meta.searchPlaceholder: technological imagination, epistemic fluency, boundary objects, double-loop learning, communities of practice, dynamic capabilities, data governance, decision packs, similarity scoring, Net Zero scenario analysis, pipeline review, uncertainty, prototype, Chiesi…
meta.userContextPlaceholder: e.g., Similar Deals team; Green Analysis scenario work; Pipeline Next review pack; participant capability; requirements gathering; hackathon planning; cross-functional collaboration; AI prompting; data governance…
meta.promptTemplate:
You are an expert designer of professional data-learning journeys in the pharmaceutical industry, with deep knowledge of organisational learning, socio-technical systems, data governance, AI prototyping and cross-functional transformation.

Use the selected lattice concepts to write a realistic account of how professional learners in Chiesi move from business ambiguity to technological imagination, data artefacts, prototype experiments and coordinated organisational action.

User context (if provided):
{{USER_CONTEXT}}

Selected concepts:
{{SELECTED_TITLES}}

Details:
{{SELECTED_DETAILS}}

Trace paths:
{{TRACE_SUMMARY}}

Deliver:
- The learning journey being traced
- The business decision or meeting being improved
- The conceptual shift in participants' understanding
- The relevant literature concepts and why they matter
- The data, AI and analytics artefacts produced
- The human judgement boundaries and uncertainty controls
- The cross-functional collaboration and adoption implications
- Two safe-to-learn experiments and the risks they should expose

levels.title: Professional purpose & organisational wisdom
levels.hint: Highest-order orientation: health and societal value, agility, stewardship, epistemic responsibility, holistic data resourcefulness and capability expansion.

levels.title: Transformative learning & technological imagination
levels.hint: Super-concepts shaping the bootcamp: technological possibility, data-informed action, responsible innovation, strategic alignment and knowledge-to-action translation.

levels.title: Socio-technical learning concepts
levels.hint: Literature concepts that explain the journey: adult/professional learning, epistemic fluency, boundary objects, communities of practice, double-loop learning, sensemaking, dynamic capabilities and sociotechnical systems.

levels.title: Organisational capability architecture
levels.hint: Structures that convert learning into capability: decision-backwards requirements, governance, shared language, minimum viable data slices, human judgement boundaries and adoption pathways.

levels.title: Bootcamp design moves & collaborative practices
levels.hint: Practical activities through which learners move from business concepts to artefacts: challenge definition, stakeholder interviews, data archaeology, storyboarding, prompting and expert validation.

levels.title: Analytical methods, artefacts & evaluation
levels.hint: Concrete data and AI capabilities: harmonisation, feature extraction, explainable similarity, baselines, scenarios, uncertainty ranges, KPI computation, flags, grounded summaries and reproducible workflows.

levels.title: Case-specific prototypes, examples & pathologies
levels.hint: Specific instances from Similar Deals, Green Analysis and Pipeline Next plus risks such as false precision, data theatre, tool-first solutionism and AI replacing judgement.

nodes.label: Health and societal value stewardship
nodes.summary: Treat data capability as a way to improve responsible pharmaceutical decision-making, not as a technical end in itself.
nodes.bodyHtml: The highest-order purpose of the bootcamp is to help Chiesi act more intelligently in service of health, sustainability, and organisational responsibility. Technical work should be evaluated by whether it improves judgement, coordination and action.

nodes.label: Organisational agility to act
nodes.summary: Develop the capacity to move from ambiguous business need to coordinated, evidence-informed action.
nodes.bodyHtml: Agility is not speed alone. It is the ability to reframe, decompose, prototype, validate and recombine knowledge across functions under uncertainty.

nodes.label: Cross-functional stewardship
nodes.summary: Use data as a shared organisational resource requiring joint ownership across business, scientific, technical and governance teams.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp positions data as something that must be stewarded across boundaries: strategy, business development, sustainability, portfolio, finance, operations, supply chain and governance.

nodes.label: Epistemic responsibility
nodes.summary: Be honest about what the evidence can and cannot support; surface uncertainty rather than polish it away.
nodes.bodyHtml: Professional judgement requires knowing the limits of data, models and AI summaries. The mature learner asks what is missing, what is inferred, what is uncertain and what still requires human review.

nodes.label: Holistic data resourcefulness
nodes.summary: See internal and external data resources as parts of a wider intelligence system rather than isolated datasets.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp expands the learner's field of possibility by connecting internal metrics, narratives, external sources, expert judgement and decision processes.

nodes.label: Learning as capability expansion
nodes.summary: Professional learning is the enlargement of what participants can notice, imagine, organise and enact with technology.
nodes.bodyHtml: The learning journey is about technical capability changing perception: once participants can build small data artefacts, previously fixed organisational problems become designable.

nodes.label: Transformative professional learning
nodes.summary: Learning that changes the learner's frame of reference, not just their tool competence.
nodes.bodyHtml: Drawing on transformative learning, the bootcamp invites participants to question taken-for-granted assumptions about meetings, evidence, data ownership, automation and decision-making.

nodes.label: Technological imagination
nodes.summary: The capacity to see business problems as potentially redesignable through data, code, models and new workflows.
nodes.bodyHtml: Technological imagination grows when learners connect conceptual business needs to concrete artefacts such as fields, rules, prompts, prototypes, outputs and validation tests.

nodes.label: Data-informed action
nodes.summary: Decision-making that connects evidence, context, uncertainty and accountable action.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp does not treat data as a passive report. It treats data work as a way of improving business conversations and enabling action.

nodes.label: Responsible innovation
nodes.summary: Anticipate, reflect, engage and act so data and AI interventions remain legitimate, useful and accountable.
nodes.bodyHtml: Responsible innovation provides a shaping discipline: anticipate consequences, reflect on assumptions, engage affected stakeholders and act through controls and learning loops.

nodes.label: Strategic value alignment
nodes.summary: Align prototypes with the decisions, meetings and business outcomes they are meant to improve.
nodes.bodyHtml: A prototype is valuable only if it improves a strategic conversation: comparator selection, Net Zero planning, pipeline review or executive prioritisation.

nodes.label: Organisational learning loop
nodes.summary: Turn prototypes, flags, feedback and expert disagreement into durable improvements in organisational practice.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp should create loops: requirements produce artefacts; artefacts produce tests; tests produce feedback; feedback changes requirements and practice.

nodes.label: Human-centred data and AI
nodes.summary: Use automation to support, not displace, professional judgement and accountability.
nodes.bodyHtml: The strongest outputs make human judgement better situated: they reveal caveats, conflicts, assumptions and next actions.

nodes.label: Knowledge-to-action translation
nodes.summary: Convert insight into changed workflow, changed conversation and changed decision behaviour.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp is successful when participants can carry learning into their teams: by creating reusable decision packs, shared definitions and repeatable workflows.

nodes.label: Andragogy and professional relevance
nodes.summary: Adult learners engage deeply when learning is problem-centred, self-directed and linked to their work.
nodes.bodyHtml: Knowles' andragogy helps explain why authentic Chiesi cases matter: professional learners need relevance, agency and immediate applicability.

nodes.label: Experiential learning cycle
nodes.summary: Learning moves through concrete experience, reflection, conceptualisation and experimentation.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp cycle mirrors Kolb: participants encounter a business problem, reflect on it, conceptualise a data workflow and test it through prototypes.

nodes.label: Reflective practitioner
nodes.summary: Professionals learn by reflecting in and on action, especially when situations are uncertain or unique.
nodes.bodyHtml: Schön's reflective practitioner is central: participants must notice breakdowns in existing practice and improvise better ways of acting with evidence.

nodes.label: Transformative learning and perspective change
nodes.summary: Learning becomes transformative when assumptions are critically examined and frames of reference change.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants may begin with a frame of reporting or tool use; the journey shifts them toward requirements, evidence, uncertainty and organisational redesign.

nodes.label: Epistemic fluency
nodes.summary: The ability to move between different ways of knowing, representing and justifying claims.
nodes.bodyHtml: Epistemic fluency helps explain the bootcamp's core movement between business narrative, domain expertise, data structure, coding, modelling and executive judgement.

nodes.label: Boundary objects
nodes.summary: Shared artefacts flexible enough for different groups yet stable enough for collaboration.
nodes.bodyHtml: Decision packs, data dictionaries, KPI definitions, similarity cards and scenario plots work as boundary objects between technical, business and domain communities.

nodes.label: Communities of practice
nodes.summary: Learning occurs through participation in shared practice, language, norms and repertoires.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp creates a temporary community of practice around Chiesi's data challenges; its value persists if participants carry shared repertoires back into departments.

nodes.label: Situated learning
nodes.summary: Knowledge is learned in the context of use, not transferred as abstract content alone.
nodes.bodyHtml: The cases situate learning inside Chiesi's decisions: inorganic growth, Net Zero evidence and pipeline review.

nodes.label: Double-loop learning
nodes.summary: Go beyond fixing errors to questioning the governing assumptions that produced them.
nodes.bodyHtml: A single-loop response fixes a spreadsheet. A double-loop response asks why definitions, ownership and decision cadence produce repeated reconciliation work.

nodes.label: Absorptive capacity
nodes.summary: The organisation's ability to recognise, assimilate and apply external knowledge.
nodes.bodyHtml: Bootcamp learning builds absorptive capacity by helping participants convert external data, AI methods and analytics practice into Chiesi-specific action.

nodes.label: Dynamic capabilities
nodes.summary: Sense, seize and transform in response to changing environments.
nodes.bodyHtml: Similar Deals supports sensing external growth patterns; Green Analysis supports seizing sustainability interventions; Pipeline Next supports transforming decision routines.

nodes.label: Sensemaking
nodes.summary: People organise ambiguity into plausible stories that support action.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp improves sensemaking by connecting narratives to data, exposing conflicts and making assumptions discussable.

nodes.label: Socio-technical systems thinking
nodes.summary: Technology and organisation co-produce performance; tools cannot be separated from work design.
nodes.bodyHtml: Every prototype changes roles, handoffs, trust and decision rhythms. Technical success depends on organisational fit.

nodes.label: Expansive learning
nodes.summary: Collective learning that reconceptualises the object of activity and creates new forms of practice.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants collectively reconceptualise 'data problem' as 'decision workflow problem', producing new artefacts and practices.

nodes.label: Tacit-explicit knowledge conversion
nodes.summary: Organisations create knowledge by moving between tacit experience and explicit representation.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp converts tacit business judgement into explicit fields, rules, prompts and diagrams, while preserving expert interpretation.

nodes.label: Design thinking and wicked problems
nodes.summary: Complex organisational problems require iterative framing, prototyping and stakeholder learning.
nodes.bodyHtml: The Chiesi cases are not simply technical puzzles; they are wicked enough to need iterative framing, stakeholder negotiation and prototypes.

nodes.label: Scaffolding and zones of proximal development
nodes.summary: Learning support should enable participants to do with guidance what they could not yet do alone.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp's technical scaffolding lets professionals move from conceptual need to data cleaning, coding, analysis and prototype design.

nodes.label: Data literacy as organisational literacy
nodes.summary: Understanding data means understanding the organisational processes, owners and incentives that produce it.
nodes.bodyHtml: A field name, missing value or inconsistent KPI is a clue to organisational process, not just a technical defect.

nodes.label: Sociomaterial practice
nodes.summary: Tools, data, bodies, routines and meanings are entangled in practice.
nodes.bodyHtml: A dashboard, prompt, spreadsheet or review pack changes what people see, say and do; the material artefact and social practice form one system.

nodes.label: Psychological safety for data learning
nodes.summary: Participants need permission to surface uncertainty, ignorance, data gaps and weak prototypes.
nodes.bodyHtml: Data learning is fragile when people fear being exposed. The bootcamp should normalise not-knowing, experimentation and challenge.

nodes.label: Decision-backwards requirements
nodes.summary: Start from the future decision or meeting and work backwards to evidence, data and prototype requirements.
nodes.bodyHtml: Each case asks: which conversation should be better after this exists? This prevents tool-first work and anchors technical choices in business use.

nodes.label: Data governance and stewardship
nodes.summary: Clarify ownership, quality, access, definitions, lineage and accountability for shared data resources.
nodes.bodyHtml: Reusable data capability requires more than analysis: it needs owners, definitions, refresh cadence, quality rules and controlled access.

nodes.label: Shared language and taxonomy
nodes.summary: Create common definitions for deals, emissions, assets, KPIs, flags, assumptions and decisions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Cross-functional action depends on a vocabulary stable enough to compute with and flexible enough to support expert judgement.

nodes.label: Minimum viable data slice
nodes.summary: Use a small, representative, trustworthy data slice to prove the concept before scaling.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful first prototype needs one focal case, a few assets or categories, a limited KPI set and realistic narratives—not every system at once.

nodes.label: Cross-functional operating model
nodes.summary: Define how business, technical, domain and governance participants work together.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp should model the cross-functional working pattern that a future data product will require.

nodes.label: Evidence pack governance
nodes.summary: Treat outputs as decision packs with sources, assumptions, confidence, caveats and action routes.
nodes.bodyHtml: A decision pack is more than a dashboard or summary: it links evidence, interpretation and responsibility.

nodes.label: Human judgement boundaries
nodes.summary: Specify which decisions can be automated, assisted or must remain expert-owned.
nodes.bodyHtml: Professional agility includes knowing where automation should stop: a flag is an invitation to inspect evidence, not a decision.

nodes.label: Data product mindset
nodes.summary: Build reusable workflows with users, quality expectations, documentation and lifecycle management.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp shifts artefacts from one-off hackathon outputs to reusable organisational capability.

nodes.label: Safe-to-learn experiment portfolio
nodes.summary: Use small experiments to expose assumptions and risks without committing prematurely to a full system.
nodes.bodyHtml: Prototype experiments should be small enough to fail safely and rich enough to change the team's understanding.

nodes.label: Auditability, lineage and provenance
nodes.summary: Make sources, transformations, assumptions, model choices and human confirmations traceable.
nodes.bodyHtml: Trustworthy pharma data work depends on knowing where evidence came from, how it was transformed and who accepted it.

nodes.label: Capability scaffolding
nodes.summary: Match technical support to participants' current readiness and the complexity of the challenge.
nodes.bodyHtml: Learners need templates, worked examples, starter notebooks, field dictionaries and coaching so that coding becomes a route into business understanding.

nodes.label: Change management and adoption pathway
nodes.summary: Plan how prototypes will fit existing tools, governance, cadences and user expectations.
nodes.bodyHtml: The point is not just to build a prototype but to make a credible path into real work.

nodes.label: Challenge definition sprint
nodes.summary: Condense the business challenge into short statements naming the decision, data and prototype aim.
nodes.bodyHtml: The Similar Deals six-line definition, Green Analysis four-sentence definition and Pipeline Next five-sentence definition turn broad intent into shareable scope.

nodes.label: Stakeholder interview sprint
nodes.summary: Interview likely users or sponsors to identify decision need, current friction and rejection criteria.
nodes.bodyHtml: A short interview can reveal what a useful output must do, what would make it credible and what would make it rejected.

nodes.label: Meeting archaeology
nodes.summary: Examine an existing review pack or meeting artefact to distinguish computed metrics, grounded narratives and judgement calls.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants mark what could be automated, what could be assisted and what must remain human-owned.

nodes.label: Data inventory and archaeology
nodes.summary: Map sources, owners, fields, update frequencies, quality concerns and readiness for hackathon use.
nodes.bodyHtml: This practice turns vague claims about data availability into a table of source, owner, cadence, key fields and quality concerns.

nodes.label: Similarity cards
nodes.summary: Rank dimensions such as scientific, commercial, financial, strategic, temporal and narrative similarity.
nodes.bodyHtml: Disagreement between experts becomes useful evidence about which assumptions the similarity model must expose.

nodes.label: Scenario marketplace
nodes.summary: Compare baseline, driver and intervention models for Green Analysis before committing to one approach.
nodes.bodyHtml: Groups can sketch alternative prototypes and trade off simplicity, explainability, uncertainty and actionability.

nodes.label: KPI dictionary workshop
nodes.summary: Define KPI name, formula, source field, owner, update cadence and interpretation.
nodes.bodyHtml: KPI work is where language becomes computable; ambiguity here will produce confident but unhelpful outputs.

nodes.label: Narrative-metric mapping
nodes.summary: Connect free-text claims to structured fields, source evidence, assumptions and contradiction checks.
nodes.bodyHtml: This practice preserves business context while making narratives inspectable and partially computable.

nodes.label: Prompting that shows its working
nodes.summary: Use AI prompts that require sources, assumptions, caveats, confidence and missing evidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: Generative AI should not merely produce fluent summaries; it should help structure evidence and reveal uncertainty.

nodes.label: Prototype backlog
nodes.summary: Convert learning questions into buildable tasks, tests and demonstrable artefacts.
nodes.bodyHtml: A good backlog item produces something inspectable: a source list, rule, prompt, notebook, mock output or validation test.

nodes.label: Peer review and demo critique
nodes.summary: Use cross-team demonstrations to test whether outputs are credible to non-builders.
nodes.bodyHtml: Demos should ask: what decision would this improve, what assumption is hidden and what would you trust or reject?

nodes.label: After-action reflection
nodes.summary: Reflect on what changed in understanding, assumptions, collaboration and prototype direction.
nodes.bodyHtml: Reflection converts hackathon activity into professional learning and organisational memory.

nodes.label: Model ladder: simple before sophisticated
nodes.summary: Build from reproducible baseline to explanation, scenarios and AI stretch goals only after foundations are sound.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp should reward clear baselines and transparent assumptions before complex AI.

nodes.label: Decision pack storyboarding
nodes.summary: Sketch the one-page output a decision audience should see, then work backwards.
nodes.bodyHtml: Storyboarding makes the desired business conversation visible before coding begins.

nodes.label: Uncertainty language design
nodes.summary: Design standard ways to describe confidence, caveats, missing data and human review needs.
nodes.bodyHtml: The organisation needs language that is neither paralysing nor falsely precise.

nodes.label: Expert validation session
nodes.summary: Ask domain experts to judge relevance, credibility, caveats and repeatability of outputs.
nodes.bodyHtml: Expert validation turns prototypes from technical demos into decision-support candidates.

nodes.label: Entity resolution and harmonisation
nodes.summary: Link records that refer to the same asset, deal, supplier, site, category or review item.
nodes.bodyHtml: Many value-creating workflows begin by asking whether records can be linked and whether terms mean the same thing across sources.

nodes.label: Feature extraction from narratives
nodes.summary: Turn announcement text, asset updates or sustainability commentary into comparable fields while retaining context.
nodes.bodyHtml: Narrative extraction can structure deal rationale, asset risks, assumptions or intervention descriptions, but must keep source evidence visible.

nodes.label: Explainable similarity scoring
nodes.summary: Rank candidates using weighted dimensions and show why a match is strong or weak.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful similarity model says: close because of scientific and strategic fit, weaker because of stage or financial structure.

nodes.label: Taxonomies and controlled vocabularies
nodes.summary: Use shared vocabularies for therapy area, modality, deal type, emissions category, asset stage and risk type.
nodes.bodyHtml: Taxonomies reduce ambiguity, improve search, support aggregation and enable cross-team comparison.

nodes.label: Forecasting baselines
nodes.summary: Start with simple baselines, trend lines, rolling averages and reference pathways before complex predictive models.
nodes.bodyHtml: Baseline models reveal whether more complex modelling adds value or simply hides assumptions.

nodes.label: Scenario and intervention analysis
nodes.summary: Test plausible future pathways and interventions with explicit assumptions and ranges.
nodes.bodyHtml: Scenario analysis supports decisions by comparing 'what might happen if' rather than pretending to know the future.

nodes.label: Uncertainty ranges and confidence indicators
nodes.summary: Represent estimation uncertainty, missingness, low confidence and boundary sensitivity.
nodes.bodyHtml: Uncertainty should be visible in forecasts, similarity pools and review packs so users know when to act, learn or improve data first.

nodes.label: Emission-factor versioning
nodes.summary: Store factor values, versions, geography and validity period so accounting revisions are not confused with operational change.
nodes.bodyHtml: Versioning allows Green Analysis to distinguish real performance from changes in emission factors or reporting boundaries.

nodes.label: Reproducible KPI computation
nodes.summary: Calculate KPIs from agreed formulas, source fields and update cadences.
nodes.bodyHtml: Reproducible KPIs reduce meeting time spent reconciling numbers and increase trust in review packs.

nodes.label: Inconsistency flags
nodes.summary: Detect missing, stale, contradictory, out-of-range or narrative-metric mismatches.
nodes.bodyHtml: Flags should invite expert inspection and escalation; they should not silently become decisions.

nodes.label: Grounded summary generation
nodes.summary: Generate summaries linked to evidence, caveats and review status rather than unsupported fluent text.
nodes.bodyHtml: Generated summaries are useful only when grounded in source data and structured to expose unresolved conflicts.

nodes.label: Dashboard versus decision pack
nodes.summary: Distinguish showing values from preparing a decision conversation.
nodes.bodyHtml: Dashboards show selected values; decision packs connect evidence, narrative, uncertainty, judgement and next actions.

nodes.label: Good-enough evaluation criteria
nodes.summary: Define how the team will know that a ranking, forecast or flag is credible enough for the next experiment.
nodes.bodyHtml: Early prototypes need realistic success measures: expert relevance, repeatability, time saved, fewer conflicts or improved discussion quality.

nodes.label: Data quality flags
nodes.summary: Record missingness, estimated values, stale updates, unit inconsistencies, duplicates and inferred fields.
nodes.bodyHtml: Quality flags make the condition of evidence visible and prevent weak data from being mistaken for strong insight.

nodes.label: Simulated and safe datasets
nodes.summary: Use fictionalised data with realistic fields, metadata and quality issues to support safe experimentation.
nodes.bodyHtml: Simulated datasets make learning possible before real data access, privacy and governance questions are fully resolved.

nodes.label: AI and ML stretch goals
nodes.summary: Use machine learning or generative AI only after basic workflow, data and validation foundations are clear.
nodes.bodyHtml: AI should extend the workflow, not rescue an unclear problem. In the bootcamp, complex models are valuable only after Levels 1-4 of the model ladder work.

nodes.label: Reproducible workflow notebooks and pipelines
nodes.summary: Create versioned scripts or notebooks that can be rerun, inspected and adapted.
nodes.bodyHtml: Reproducible workflows turn a hackathon demonstration into a reusable organisational asset.

nodes.label: Case: Similar Deals focal opportunity
nodes.summary: A focal acquisition, licensing, collaboration or asset purchase is compared with announced historical deals.
nodes.bodyHtml: The case asks which previous deals are comparable enough to inform strategic discussion and what caveats should be attached.

nodes.label: Trap: Same therapy area equals similar deal
nodes.summary: A keyword or therapy-area search returns superficial comparators and hides important differences.
nodes.bodyHtml: This trap treats labels as logic and misses stage, modality, deal type, strategic rationale, financial terms and timing.

nodes.label: Case: False-friend comparator
nodes.summary: Two deals look similar by keyword but differ strategically or structurally.
nodes.bodyHtml: A late-stage commercial acquisition and an early-stage platform collaboration may share a therapy area but support very different business inferences.

nodes.label: Prototype: Expert-labelled comparator pool
nodes.summary: One focal case, 30-100 candidate records and 5-10 expert-labelled good or poor matches.
nodes.bodyHtml: The expert-labelled pool tests whether similarity dimensions and ranking logic are business-credible.

nodes.label: Case: Green Analysis Net Zero decision
nodes.summary: Historical emissions, drivers and interventions are organised into forecasts and scenario evidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: The case asks which Net Zero decision should be improved and what evidence is needed to support it.

nodes.label: Case: Same emissions, different stories
nodes.summary: A 4% rise in emissions may reflect production, intensity, supplier, factor, weather, travel or boundary effects.
nodes.bodyHtml: The analytical task is to distinguish operational change from accounting, boundary and activity effects.

nodes.label: Case: Factor revision mistaken for progress
nodes.summary: A footprint drops because a new emissions-factor table is applied, not because operations improved.
nodes.bodyHtml: The prototype must version factors and recalculate history consistently to avoid false interpretation.

nodes.label: Case: Supplier-category prioritisation
nodes.summary: The largest estimated emissions category may have low confidence or limited organisational influence.
nodes.bodyHtml: A better decision separates estimated emissions, confidence and ability to influence.

nodes.label: Case: Pipeline Next review pack
nodes.summary: Asset metrics, narratives and assumptions are combined into a reproducible review pack.
nodes.bodyHtml: The case asks what changed, whether data is consistent, which assets need attention and what decision follows.

nodes.label: Case: Slow review meeting
nodes.summary: A review spends time reconciling a spreadsheet, slide narrative and risk log rather than making decisions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Pipeline Next should surface mismatches before the meeting so expert review focuses on judgement rather than data repair.

nodes.label: Trap: Fluent summary hides unresolved conflict
nodes.summary: AI-generated text sounds polished while data conflicts remain unresolved.
nodes.bodyHtml: The danger is not poor writing; it is persuasive writing that conceals uncertainty, inconsistency or missing evidence.

nodes.label: Prototype: Asset conflict flag
nodes.summary: An asset has conflicting status, milestone and risk evidence and is flagged for expert review.
nodes.bodyHtml: This prototype tests whether the workflow can detect contradiction and route it to human confirmation.

nodes.label: Pathology: Data theatre
nodes.summary: Clean-looking dashboards and charts create the appearance of insight without improving decisions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Data theatre occurs when presentation substitutes for evidence, interpretation and action.

nodes.label: Pathology: Tool-first solutionism
nodes.summary: The team begins with AI, dashboards or models before the decision and evidence need are clear.
nodes.bodyHtml: Tool-first work produces impressive but misaligned outputs; decision-backwards requirements counteract it.

nodes.label: Pathology: Siloed dataset ownership
nodes.summary: Departments protect local datasets and definitions, preventing holistic analysis and shared action.
nodes.bodyHtml: Silos undermine synergy because the evidence chain crosses organisational boundaries.

nodes.label: Pathology: False precision
nodes.summary: Exact-looking numbers or rankings conceal estimated, missing, changing or uncertain inputs.
nodes.bodyHtml: False precision is especially dangerous in forecasts, comparator rankings and executive summaries.

nodes.label: Pathology: AI replaces judgement
nodes.summary: Automation is treated as a decision-maker rather than a support for evidence inspection.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp must reinforce that similarity scores, flags and generated summaries invite professional judgement.

nodes.label: Instance: Similar Deals six-line definition
nodes.summary: Define focal case, decision, useful comparator, misleading comparator, intended help and non-use.
nodes.bodyHtml: This activity forces the team to define similarity in relation to a business decision.

nodes.label: Instance: Green Analysis four-sentence definition
nodes.summary: Define decision, emissions question, trust basis and forbidden use.
nodes.bodyHtml: This activity prevents generic sustainability discussion and makes the forecast/scenario purpose explicit.

nodes.label: Instance: Pipeline Next five-sentence definition
nodes.summary: Define review to improve, main decision, core sources, key inconsistency and prototype aim.
nodes.bodyHtml: This activity converts slow review pain into a testable workflow.

nodes.label: Instance: Five-column data inventory
nodes.summary: Source, owner, update frequency, key fields and quality concerns.
nodes.bodyHtml: This table makes data readiness visible and discussable.

nodes.label: Instance: One-page decision pack
nodes.summary: A concise output showing evidence, assumptions, caveats, confidence and next actions.
nodes.bodyHtml: This is the shared artefact through which technical work changes a business conversation.
